conversation.text_input:
Description
In the following MWE, setting a global mesh and doing some complex indexing inside of a linear solve triggers some hard-to-decode error deep into jax.
not setting the global mesh or using float32 tensors will lead to no issues.
FYI, I'm pretty sure this was not crashing on jax@main ~2 weeks ago.

import jax.numpy as jnp

jax.sharding.set_mesh(mesh)

param_dtype = jnp.complex64

issue_title: Inconsistent Reduction precision in backwards computation

conversation.text_input:
Description
JAX implicitly upcasts BF16 inputs to jnp.sum to FP32 (see here). However, such reductions are also generated automatically in the backward pass for things like broadcasts. In this case, BF16 reductions are used, which can be highly unstable. This is inconsistent with the implicit upcasting of jnp.sum.
A simple example of the grad of a broadcast:
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

x = jnp.ones((128, 128), dtype=jnp.bfloat16)

def f(x, a):
  out = jnp.sin(x * a).astype(jnp.float32)
  return jnp.sum(out)

f_grad = jax.jit(jax.grad(f, argnums=(0, 1)))
f_grad.lower(x, 2.3).as_text()

gives a BF16 reduction:
    %8 = stablehlo.reduce(%7 init: %cst_0) applies stablehlo.add across dimensions = [0, 1] : (tensor<128x128xbf16>, tensor<bf16>) -> tensor<bf16>

FP32 upcasting for reductions should be used consistently (both for jnp.sum but also reductions in the backward pass), but ideally, should be controllable via a context manager.
System info (python version, jaxlib version, accelerator, etc.)
Not relevant.

It would appear this is in part due to the jit=bool parameter that most of the jaxopt solvers use, which is True by default and so the full optimisation loop attempts compilation, but due to the outer vmap, we are obviously passing around Tracers to an underlying jitted function.

Hi - thanks for the question! The operative difference here is that in run_loop, N is static, and so the fori_loop lowers to a scan. In run_loop_jit, N is dynamic, and so it lowers to while_loop. scan is generally faster than while_loop because the compiler can better optimize when the number of iterations is known at compile time.
If you want to JIT-compile your function without changing the lowering path of the loop, you can mark N as static in your JIT compilation:
run_loop_jit = jax.jit(run_loop, static_argnames=["N"])

issue_title: Add nn.logmeanexp

conversation.text_input:
Add to jax.nn a function logmeanexp, analogous to logsumexp, that computes
$$ \text{logmeanexp}(x) = \log \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \exp x_i = \text{logsumexp}(x) - \log n $$
Some nontrivial code is needed to get the $\log n$ term right, as for mean. (For example, when axis is a tuple, or there is a where mask, or keepdims is used.)1
This function is defined in other libraries:

https://www.tensorflow.org/probability/api_docs/python/tfp/math/reduce_logmeanexp
https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/pomp/versions/6.3/topics/logmeanexp
https://botorch.readthedocs.io/en/stable/utils.html#botorch.utils.safe_math.logmeanexp

It is also used to define the mellowmax operator:
$$ \text{mellowmax}_\omega(x) = \text{logmeanexp}(x \omega) / \omega $$
Here are some works that use MellowMax:

An alternative softmax operator for reinforcement learning (2016)
Revisiting the softmax Bellman operator: New benefits and new perspective (2018)
DeepMellow: removing the need for a target network in deep Q-learning (2019)
Adaptive temperature tuning for Mellowmax in deep reinforcement learning (2019)
Sample-efficient reinforcement learning with maximum entropy mellowmax episodic control (2019)
Stabilizing Q learning via soft Mellowmax operator (2020)
Damped Anderson mixing for deep reinforcement learning: Acceleration, convergence, and stabilization (2021)
A weighted smooth Q-Learning algorithm (2025)

1 Perhaps it's worth defining a generic count(array, *, axis=None, where=None, keepdims=False) function that can be used by both mean and logmeanexp, and handles the broadcasting correctly? This would simplify their implementations to
def mean(array, *, axis=None, where=None, keepdims=False):
  s = sum(array, axis=axis, where=where, keepdims=keepdims)
  c = count(array, axis=axis, where=where, keepdims=keepdims)
  return s / c

def logmeanexp(array, *, axis=None, where=None, keepdims=False):
  lse = logsumexp(array, axis=axis, where=where, keepdims=keepdims)
  c = count(array, axis=axis, where=where, keepdims=keepdims)
  return lse - log(c)

Hey, thanks for reporting this! I think the issue is that it's not clear what the broadcasting semantics of poly operations is meant to be: jax is only designed and tested for 1D inputs, though it implicitly supports multi-dimensional inputs via normal broadcasting rules when the shapes align.
NumPy also supports N-dimensional inputs, but the docs suggest this is unintentional:

I can imagine a few fixes here:

Update JAX to match the unintentional broadcasting semantics of NumPy for non-1D inputs.
Update JAX to work correctly over batched inputs, whether or not the resulting behavior matches the unintentional semantics of NumPy.
Update JAX to raise an explicit error for non-1D inputs.

issue_title: Gradient of gather uses 2x to 4x memory

conversation.text_input:
Description
I have a simple gather operation x[tuples] I want to apply autodiff to. But using jax.grad on the function uses 2x or 4x as much memory as the original function.
This might be a bug in XLA instead of JAX, but I am reporting it here as it happens easily using JAX.
This is a simple example showing the issue:
import os
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

grads = sys.argv[1] == "grads"
mode = "grads" if grads else "nograds"

out_dir = f"tmp_dump/{mode}"

os.environ["XLA_FLAGS"] = f"--xla_dump_to={out_dir}"

idx = jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((2048 * 2048 * 2048, 3), jnp.int32) # or jnp.int16

x = jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((128, 128, 128), jnp.float32)

def function_using_idx(x, idx):
    tuples = tuple(jnp.split(idx, indices_or_sections=3, axis=-1))
    gathered = x[tuples][..., 0]
    return jnp.sum(gathered * 2.5)

if grads:
    function_using_idx = jax.grad(function_using_idx, argnums=0)

hlo = jax.jit(function_using_idx).lower(x, idx).compile()

mem_report = Path(out_dir) / "module_0001.jit_function_using_idx.cpu_after_optimizations-memory-usage-report.txt"

with mem_report.open() as f:
    print(next(f),end="")
 ➜  ~ python trivial_idx.py nograds
Total bytes used: 138521083996 (129.01GiB)
 ➜  ~ python trivial_idx.py grads
Total bytes used: 240526557204 (224.01GiB)

Using those array sizes, the function input idx (s32[8589934592,3]) is 96GB large and the intermediate gathered (f32[8589934592]) is 32GB large. The regular jitted function can run with only 1GB additional memory at the peak (data from buffer-assignment.txt:

conversation.text_input:
Description
Based on the concepts explained in https://docs.jax.dev/en/latest/jax.experimental.custom_partitioning.html it is possible to create a sharded version of a 3D rfftn that never stores the full array on one GPU.
But when trying to use autodiff on this function, I fail to find a way to get the compiler to avoid collecting the array on one GPU (which is not possible for very large input arrays and number of GPUs)
The original implementation from the custom_partitioning fails with

This is the main implementation of the custom_partitioning implementing a slab decomposition (splitting the rfftn into a rfft along the Z axis and a fftn along X and Y) with the added custom_vjp:
from typing import Callable  
  
import jax.distributed  
from jax.debug import inspect_array_sharding  
from jax.experimental.custom_partitioning import custom_partitioning  
from jax.sharding import NamedSharding, PartitionSpec as P  
  
try:  
    from jax_array_info import sharding_info  
except ModuleNotFoundError:  
    sharding_info = lambda x,name: inspect_array_sharding(x, callback=print)  
  
def fft_partitioner(fft_func: Callable[[jax.Array], jax.Array], partition_spec: P, sharding_rule=None):  
    @jax.custom_batching.sequential_vmap  
    @custom_partitioning    def func(x):  
        return fft_func(x)  
  
    def supported_sharding(sharding, shape):  
        assert sharding is not None  
        return NamedSharding(sharding.mesh, partition_spec)  
  
    def partition(mesh, arg_shapes, result_shape):  
        arg_shardings = jax.tree.map(lambda x: x.sharding, arg_shapes)  
        return mesh, fft_func, supported_sharding(arg_shardings[0], arg_shapes[0]), (  
            supported_sharding(arg_shardings[0], arg_shapes[0]),)  
  
    def infer_sharding_from_operands(mesh, arg_shapes, result_shape):  
        arg_shardings = jax.tree.map(lambda x: x.sharding, arg_shapes)  
        return supported_sharding(arg_shardings[0], arg_shapes[0])  
  
    func.def_partition(  
        infer_sharding_from_operands=infer_sharding_from_operands,  
        partition=partition,  
        sharding_rule=sharding_rule  
    )  
    return func

issue_title: Inefficient 1D convolution compared to PyTorch

conversation.text_input:
Description
I wrote a small benchmark comparing a 1D depthwise convolution implemented in PyTorch vs. pure JAX on GPU, and found that the JAX version is both substantially slower (≈3×) and draws noticeably more power than the equivalent PyTorch call.
import time
import torch
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np


def jax_conv1d(inputs, kernel, bias=None):
    """Pure JAX 1D depthwise convolution benchmark"""
    output = jax.lax.conv_general_dilated(
        lhs=inputs,
        rhs=kernel,
        window_strides=(1,),
        padding='SAME',
        dimension_numbers=('NLC', 'LIO', 'NLC'),
        feature_group_count=inputs.shape[-1]
    )
    if bias is not None:
        output = output + bias
    return output


def main():
    # Benchmark parameters
    batch_size, dim, length = 128, 256, 512
    device = torch.device('cuda')

    # PyTorch setup
    torch_input = torch.randn(batch_size, dim, length, device=device)
    dwconv_pt = torch.nn.Conv1d(dim, dim, 3, padding=1, groups=dim).to(device)

    # JAX setup
    jax.config.update('jax_platform_name', 'gpu')
    np_input = np.random.randn(batch_size, length, dim).astype('float32')
    jax_input = jnp.array(np_input)
    kernel = jax.random.normal(jax.random.PRNGKey(0), (3, 1, dim)) * 0.1

    # Warm-up
    for _ in range(10):
        dwconv_pt(torch_input)
        jax_conv1d(jax_input, kernel).block_until_ready()

    # Timing
    torch_time, jax_time = 0.0, 0.0
    runs = 50
    for _ in range(runs):
        # PyTorch timing
        start = time.time()
        dwconv_pt(torch_input)
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        torch_time += time.time() - start

        # JAX timing
        start = time.time()
        out = jax_conv1d(jax_input, kernel)
        out.block_until_ready()
        jax_time += time.time() - start

    print(f"PyTorch Conv1d: {torch_time / runs * 1000:.3f} ms")
    print(f"JAX Conv1d: {jax_time / runs * 1000:.3f} ms")


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
Output:
PyTorch Conv1d: 0.269 ms
JAX Conv1d: 0.802 ms

Profiling shows that PyTorch convolution dispatches the conv_depthwise2d_forward_kernel_generic kernel (179us), whereas JAX/XLA generates the conv2d_grouped_direct_kernel kernel (517us).

issue_title: Decorator versions of pure_callback and io_callback

conversation.text_input:
It would be convenient to have decorator versions of pure_callback and io_callback. Example:
import pickle
import jax

@jax.io_callback(None)
def callback(epoch, metrics):
    print(f"epoch {epoch} loss: {metrics["loss"]:g}")
    path = f"metrics/{epoch}.pickle"
    with open(path, "wb") as file:
        pickle.dump(metrics, file)
In addition to the advantages of the decorator syntax, this removes any ambiguity between the constructor's arguments and the callback's arguments. That is, argument names like callback, result_shape_dtypes, args, vectorized, vmap_method, sharding, ordered, and kwargs can be used by the callback function.
Furthermore, this allows one to add further arguments in the future to pure_callback and io_callback without breaking backward compatibility (by overlapping with argument names that users are already using in their callbacks). Likewise for removing arguments, which currently would lead to them unintentionally being passed as **kwargs to the callback.
Finally, aesthetically, this seems to fit better with JAX's function transformation paradigm/philosophy (jit, vmap, grad, etc.).

issue_title: jax.numpy.from_dlpack warns for unaligned data

conversation.text_input:
Description
Converting numpy arrays to jax arrays using from_dlpack prints out warnings that cannot be silenced if the numpy array buffer is not aligned according to XLA's requirements. There should be a way to either suppress these warnings or make them configurable.
Consider the following code
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np

x_np = np.arange(10, dtype=np.float32)
x_jax = jnp.from_dlpack(x_np)
# 2025-06-27 16:12:33.499723: W jaxlib/dlpack.cc:230] DLPack buffer is not aligned (data at: 0x55e58c37c090). Creating a copy.
We can of course force the alignment of the array manually using
x_np = np.arange(10, dtype=np.float32)
x_np = np.asarray(jnp.asarray(x_np), copy=True)  # Prevent readonly array errors
x_jax = jnp.from_dlpack(x_np)
# No warning because XLA alignment works out
but doing so defeats the purpose of having a general sharing mechanism between frameworks. In addition, the Python Array API specifies:

from_dlpack(x: object, /, *, device: device | None = None, copy: bool | None = None) → array
copy (Optional[bool]) – boolean indicating whether or not to copy the input. If True, the function must always copy. If False, the function must never copy, and raise BufferError in case a copy is deemed necessary (e.g. if a cross-device data movement is requested, and it is not possible without a copy). If None, the function must reuse the existing memory buffer if possible and copy otherwise. Default: None.
(Link)

so there is no reason for users to assume that from_dlpack must be zero-copy, and hence no reason to warn in these cases. Displaying warnings on copies would be a nice opt-in feature, although one can argue that users should just use from_dlpack(..., copy=False) if cases where this is intended to be strictly inforced.

Converting numpy arrays to jax arrays using from_dlpack prints out warnings that cannot be silenced if the numpy array buffer is not aligned according to XLA's requirements. There should be a way to either suppress these warnings or make them configurable.

Suppressing such warnings makes sense to me. In fact, using copy= in from_dlpack is sufficient to control cases of forced-copy (copy=True), require-zero-copy (copy=False), and copy-on-the-need (copy=None) that makes the warning superfluous.
OT: Ideally, there should be way to specify the data alignment requirements when creating a numpy array, something similar to NEP 49 but at the Python level.

issue_title: partial_eval.close_jaxpr cache is leaking

conversation.text_input:
Description
The partial_eval.close_jaxpr cache is a util.weakref_lru_cache (the first argument of the key is a weakref). Since the function maps jaxpr to ClosedJaxpr(jaxpr, ()) even though the jaxpr key is a weakref, the value has a strong ref to the same jaxpr so the cache is never cleared, as shown by this test:
  def test_pe_close_jaxpr_cache(self):
    @jax.jit
    def f(x):
      return x

    pe.close_jaxpr.cache_clear()
    jaxpr = f.trace(0.).jaxpr
    keys_1 = pe.close_jaxpr.cache_keys()
    self.assertGreater(len(keys_1), 0)
    del jaxpr
    keys_2 = pe.close_jaxpr.cache_keys()
    self.assertEqual(len(keys_2), 0)  # FAILS 1 != 0

This is actually a (subtle) problem, because some of the Jaxpr that end up being kept live end up hanging on to other large objects, such as executables (most likely through other caches).
For example, if one changes (here):
  core.ClosedJaxpr(jaxpr, consts)

to
  core.ClosedJaxpr(jaxpr, consts) if consts else pe.close_jaxpr(jaxpr)

we should expect no behavior change. But instead the test api_test.test_jit_cache_clear fails with one executable being leaked. This is because we now use pe.close_jaxpr on a top-level JIT, which is used as cache keys for lowering and executables. I have also seen SEGFAULT in some internal Google tests if I make this change, presumably also because of changes to the lifetimes of objects.

issue_title: `jax.block_until_ready()` should error on non-arrays by default

conversation.text_input:
Description
jax.block_until_ready() works on arbitrary pytrees, and will silently ignore any object in the pytree which is not a jax array.
This can lead to surprises if something is not registered as a pytree by mistake or the wrong object is passed to the function: in that case, block_until_ready will silently noop. It took me a while to figure out a bug that was caused by something like the following:
import jax

class Foo:  # forgot to register this as pytree, oops
    def __init__(self):
        self.x = ...  # some expensive jax computation

jax.block_until_ready(Foo())  # this silently does not block

# unexpected behavior downstream of here...
I think this behavior should be opt-in rather than the default (like in the original version #8536), something like:
jax.block_until_ready(object())  # DeprecationWarning
jax.block_until_ready(object(), strict=True)  # raise exception
jax.block_until_ready(object(), strict=False)  # ok

issue_title: Large memory increase when performing operation on diagonal of kronecker product vs kronecker product directly

conversation.text_input:
Description
When getting the gradient of functions involving the diagonal of the kronecker product there is a significant increase in vram usage. In some rough tests anywhere from 2x -10x .
In the example below in my case changing the operation from being performed on the matrix vs the diagonal of the matrix changes my VRAM usage from ~160MB to 2200MB.
I also printed out the jaxpr instructions and noticed the number of lines of instructions for the non diagonal case was 102. For the diagonal case (high memory usage case)  was 241.
The VRAM usage only seems to increase when taking the gradient and when using the kronecker. If I just do the mean of the diagonal/the mean on a parameter array passed in to the loss function, no change in memory usage.
import os
os.environ["XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE"] = "0"
import jax.numpy as jnp
import jax

import optax


HIGH_MEMORY = False # CHANGE THIS TO ENABLE/DISABLE HIGH MEMORY USAGE


def compute_loss(params):
    loss = jnp.kron(params, jnp.eye(200))
    return jnp.sum(jnp.diagonal(loss)) if HIGH_MEMORY else jnp.sum(loss)


key = jax.random.PRNGKey(42)

start_learning_rate = 1e-1
optimizer = optax.adam(start_learning_rate)
params = jax.random.normal(key=key, shape=(100,100))

The main difference here is that sum is a single XLA primitive, while extracting the diagonal of an array is a compound operation built from a number of XLA primitives. So it's not surprising that using sum(diag(x)) rather than sum(x) would result in a longer jaxpr, more operations, and more memory consumption.

Yes, it picks it up from the mesh context and that's true for all jax ops.
Generally speaking, you need to be explicit about shardings and how arrays are sharded. I agree that in some places we allow empty meshes while for dot we don't but dot is complicated so it has more strict rules than other primitives.
For example, in the np_inp @ jax_array, if we allow this then the transpose rule for dot will set out_sharding when we transpose LHS to empty but that's not what you will get when you actual do a grad. You will see a fully replicated jax.Array out with a replicated sharding (not an empty mesh).
These kinds of things make it harder to justify supporting empty mesh for dot but the rules are straightforward if you are being explicit about your shardings!

issue_title: [jet] use proper Taylor coefficients during calculation

conversation.text_input:
In Evaluating Derivatives (Griewank & Walther, §13) the Taylor series in the Taylor propagation approach (i.e., jet) is
$f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n x^n,$
where $a_n$ is called the n-th Taylor coefficient.
jax.experimental.jet instead propagates the factorial-scaled value
$c_n=n! \cdot a_n$ and calls $c_n$ as the Taylor coefficient in the docs.
While this makes the output of jet interpretable as an ordinary n-th order derivative of $f$, it forces extra scaling/un-scaling by $n!$, which can overflow or amplify rounding error due to the use of factorial (see #9712);
Proposal: propagate the unscaled coefficients $a_n$ internally and (optionally) offer a compatibility flag/wrapper current for the n! convention.
Below is a comparison of the exponential rule before and after this change:
# Current jet implementation
def _exp_taylor(primals_in, series_in, **_):
  x, = primals_in
  series, = series_in
  u = [x] + series
  v = [lax.exp(x)] + [None] * len(series)
  for k in range(1,len(v)):
    v[k] = fact(k-1) * sum(_scale(k, j) * v[k-j] * u[j] for j in range(1, k+1))
  primal_out, *series_out = v
  return primal_out, series_out
jet_rules[lax.exp_p] = _exp_taylor
# Using "true" Taylor coefficient
def _exp_taylor(primals_in, series_in, **_):
  x, = primals_in
  series, = series_in
  u = [x] + series
  v = [lax.exp(x)] + [None] * len(series)
  for k in range(1, len(v)):
    v[k] = sum(j * v[k - j] * u[j] for j in range(1, k + 1)) / k
  primal_out, *series_out = v
  return primal_out, series_out
After this change, it would also offer jet the possibility to switch to a scan/vmap implementation, to avoid all the python for-loop unrolling --- currently, because of these unrolling, realistically, one can only go to up to about 10-th order derivative before the XLA compiler hangs. One can see that the code like fact(k-1) makes it awkward, though not impossible, to implement everything without python for-loops.
I have implemented some of these changes locally already. I raised the issue to ask if the maintainers would be interested in a PR? Are there any downside to such an unscaled approach?

issue_title: ravel_pytree does not support uint32 type (and PRNGKey as a consequence)

conversation.text_input:
Description
Dear Sirs,
Hi there. ravel_pytree seems to truncate integers larger than 2**31 if the pytree has mixed integer and floating-point types. I have found a workaround with lax::bitcast_convert_type to f32, see below. This affects for example storing PRNG keys in flattened pytrees (I bumped into this problem while trying to freeze randomness between unrolling a trajectory and learning from a replay buffer, which is a mixed-type flattened pytree).
import jax
from jax import numpy as jnp, flatten_util, lax
pt = {'foo': jnp.array([2**31 + 1], dtype=jnp.uint32), 'bar': jnp.array([2.])}

flat, unflatten = flatten_util.ravel_pytree(pt)

unflatten(flat)['foo'][0].astype(jnp.uint32)  # prints 2**31

Workaround by casting with lax::bitcast_convert_type to float32:
pt2 = {'foo': lax.bitcast_convert_type(jnp.array([2**31 + 1], dtype=jnp.uint32), jnp.float32), 'bar': jnp.array([2.])}
flat2, unflatten2 = flatten_util.ravel_pytree(pt2)
lax.bitcast_convert_type(unflatten2(flat2)['foo'][0], jnp.uint32)  # prints 2**31+1

It also works if I change the type of bar to an integer (but this is less practical because my real pytree has mostly floating-point numbers and a small number of uint32s rather than the other way round):
pt = {'foo': jnp.array([2**31 + 1], dtype=jnp.uint32), 'bar': jnp.array([2])}
flat, unflatten = flatten_util.ravel_pytree(pt)
unflatten(flat)['foo'][0].astype(jnp.uint32)  # prints 2**31+1

conversation.output:
Unfortunately I think this is working as expected. The semantics of ravel_pytree are to convert inputs to a common type, and when X64 is disabled there is no floating point type available with enough precision to handle the full uint32 range.
You could work around this by enabling 64-bit types in which case the raveled array will use float64 (see https://docs.jax.dev/en/latest/default_dtypes.html):
import jax
jax.config.update('jax_enable_x64', True)

from jax import numpy as jnp, flatten_util, lax
pt = {'foo': jnp.array([2**31 + 1], dtype=jnp.uint32), 'bar': jnp.array([2.])}

flat, unflatten = flatten_util.ravel_pytree(pt)

unflatten(flat)['foo'][0].astype(jnp.uint32)  # prints 2**31 + 1
But of course that would fail with large uint64 values for the same reason.
Overall, if your code is sensitive to these kinds of precision issues, it's probably best to avoid routines like ravel_pytree that coerce all data to a common type.

issue_title: In lax.scan, let unroll=0 unroll the whole loop

conversation.text_input:
It would be convenient to have an integer value for the unroll argument of lax.scan that unrolls the whole loop. (As opposed to the unergonomic and confusing situation of having to switch between integers and the boolean True, not to be confused with 1, which is confusingly equivalent to False.)
I argue that 0 would be a natural choice for such a value.
unroll=n splits a sequence of size k into chunks of size n followed by a chunk of size k mod n.
Thus unroll=0 should split a sequence of size k into chunks of size 0 (i.e. nothing) followed by a chunk of size k mod 0.
But k mod 0 == k. (See, e.g., here, here, here, and here.)
Therefore, unroll=0 should split a sequence into nothing followed by a chunk of size k (i.e., the whole sequence).
If this proposal is agreeable, I can create a short PR for this.

For more context, I develop a JAX package for scientific application (https://github.com/mjo22/cryojax/). issue_title: [lax.map] Map over multiple arguments

conversation.text_input:
The current definition of lax.map is
jax.lax.map(f: Callable, xs: Array, *, batch_size: int|None=None)
which maps the function f across the elements xs[I] such that lax.map(f, xs) == np.stack([f(x) for x in xs]) .
oftentimes I find myself in need of a map function that maps across multiple arguments, similar to what jax.tree.map does.
I would like to put forth the feature request of supporting a variable number of arguments
jax.lax.map(f: Callable, *xs: Array, *, batch_size: int|None=None)
such that
lax.map(f, xs, ys) == np.stack([f(x, y) for x,y in zip(xs, ys)]) 
In particular, it would be useful if the batch_size argument worked well with this setting.

def transform_log_normal(z, mu, sigma):
    return jax.lax.exp(mu + sigma*z)
def transform_logit_normal(z, scale, mu, sigma):
    return scale * 1 / (1 + jax.lax.exp(-(mu + sigma*z)))
def transform_param(field: str, z):
    if field == "gamma":
        return transform_logit_normal(z, 2, 0, 1)
    else:
        return transform_log_normal(z, -1.5, 1.)
    
@dataclass
class SquaredExponential():
    lengthscale: jax.Array
    amplitude: jax.Array
    def eval_cov_vec(self, ts: jax.Array) -> jax.Array:
        dt = ts.reshape(-1,1) - ts.reshape(1,-1)
        c = jax.lax.exp(-0.5 * dt * dt / jax.lax.square(self.lengthscale))
        return self.amplitude * c
    
def logdensity(x):
    lengthscale = transform_param("lengthscale", x[0])
    amplitude = transform_param("amplitude", x[1])
    noise = transform_param("noise", x[2]) + 1e-5
    lp = jax.scipy.stats.norm.logpdf(lengthscale) + jax.scipy.stats.norm.logpdf(amplitude) + jax.scipy.stats.norm.logpdf(noise)
    k = SquaredExponential(lengthscale, amplitude)
    cov_matrix = k.eval_cov_vec(xs) + noise * jnp.eye(xs.size)
    return lp + jax.scipy.stats.multivariate_normal.logpdf(ys, jax.lax.zeros_like_array(xs), cov_matrix)


OPTIMIZER_STATE = TypeVar("OPTIMIZER_STATE")
OPTIMIZER_PARAMS = jax.Array
OPTIMIZER_UPDATES = jax.Array


class Optimizer(NamedTuple, Generic[OPTIMIZER_STATE]):
    init_fn: Callable[[OPTIMIZER_PARAMS], OPTIMIZER_STATE]
    update_fn: Callable[[int, OPTIMIZER_UPDATES,
                         OPTIMIZER_STATE], OPTIMIZER_STATE]
    get_params_fn: Callable[[OPTIMIZER_STATE], OPTIMIZER_PARAMS]

def Adam(step_size: float, b1=0.9, b2=0.999, eps=1e-8) -> Optimizer:

    def init(x0: jax.Array) -> Tuple[jax.Array, jax.Array, jax.Array]:
        m0 = jnp.zeros_like(x0)
        v0 = jnp.zeros_like(x0)
        return x0, m0, v0

    def update(i: int, g: jax.Array, state: Tuple[jax.Array, jax.Array, jax.Array]):
        x, m, v = state
        m = (1 - b1) * g + b1 * m  # First  moment estimate.
        v = (1 - b2) * jnp.square(g) + b2 * v  # Second moment estimate.
        # Bias correction.
        mhat = m / (1 - jnp.asarray(b1, m.dtype) ** (i + 1))
        vhat = v / (1 - jnp.asarray(b2, m.dtype) ** (i + 1))
        x = x - step_size * mhat / (jnp.sqrt(vhat) + eps)
        return x, m, v

    def get_params(state: Tuple[jax.Array, jax.Array, jax.Array]) -> jax.Array:
        x, _, _ = state
        return x
    return Optimizer(init, update, get_params)


class Meanfield:
    def __init__(self, X, init_sigma: float = 1.) -> None:
        flat_X, unravel_fn = jax.flatten_util.ravel_pytree(X)
        self.n_latents = flat_X.shape[0]
        self.mu = jax.lax.zeros_like_array(flat_X)
        self.omega = jax.lax.full_like(flat_X, jnp.log(init_sigma))
        self.unravel_fn = unravel_fn
    def get_params(self) -> jax.Array:
       return jax.lax.concatenate((self.mu, self.omega), 0)
    def update_params(self, params: jax.Array):
       self.mu = params[:self.n_latents]
       self.omega = params[self.n_latents:]
    def sample_and_log_prob(self, rng_key, shape = ()) -> Tuple[jax.Array, jax.Array]:
        z = jax.random.normal(rng_key, self.mu.shape)
        x = self.mu + jax.lax.exp(self.omega) * z
        return self.unravel_fn(x), jax.scipy.stats.norm.logpdf(z).sum()

class ADVIState(NamedTuple, Generic[OPTIMIZER_STATE]):
    iteration: int
    optimizer_state: OPTIMIZER_STATE

def make_advi_step(logdensity, guide: Meanfield, optimizer: Optimizer[OPTIMIZER_STATE]):
    def elbo_fn(params: jax.Array, rng_key) -> jax.Array:
        guide.update_params(params)
        X, lq = guide.sample_and_log_prob(rng_key)
        lp = logdensity(X)
        elbo = lp - lq
        return elbo
    
    def advi_step(advi_state: ADVIState[OPTIMIZER_STATE], rng_key) -> Tuple[ADVIState[OPTIMIZER_STATE], jax.Array]:
        iteration, optimizer_state = advi_state
        params = optimizer.get_params_fn(optimizer_state)
        elbo, elbo_grad = jax.value_and_grad(elbo_fn, argnums=0)(params, rng_key)
        new_optimizer_state = optimizer.update_fn(iteration, -elbo_grad, optimizer_state)
        return ADVIState(iteration + 1, new_optimizer_state), elbo
    
    return advi_step

  key1, key2 = jax.random.split(key)
  val = val + jax.random.normal(key1)
  return (val,key2), None

It's the difference between how JAX uses XLA on macOS vs. Linux. I know on Linux, XLA is more aggressively parallelizing even if adds more iterations. I'm not too sure about macOS, but if I remember correctly, it uses fewer threads by default because macOS has something built in specifically (I don't remember the exact name). There is also an Output difference with task set due to the float point being non-deterministic in multithreading, causing different thread interleaving, which then causes different instruction ordering. Slighting changing in computation order leading to a bit level difference in float points. This semi expected (I think) since it's just how parallelism is with non-associative arithmetic.


Try limiting XLA to use fewer threads
export XLA_FLAGS="--xla_cpu_multi_thread_eigen=false intra_op_parallelism_threads=1"


You could also pass threads count dynamically
os.environ["XLA_FLAGS"] = "--xla_cpu_multi_thread_eigen=false intra_op_parallelism_threads=1"`


I'll look into actual fixes later

You cannot do a dynamic slice on an array that has already been loaded from a Ref (this is a compiler limitation). However, you can load from a Ref with a dynamic start index.
I think the correct solution here is to add dynamic start index support to the aqt_pl.load_qtensor function you are using the load the Ref. Looking at the AQT library, I believe you can just thread the slices into the function here.

conversation.output:
A couple specific replies here:


having numpy arrays vs jnp arrays in the tree structure


If you have NumPy arrays in your tree structure, then each time the structure is passed to a JIT-compiled function, every array in your structure will be converted to an on-device JAX array. If your structure has many such arrays, this could account for some of the call-time overhead.


setting arrays as static (by storing them as multiple floats)


This may speed up a particular call by avoiding device transfer, but keep in mind that every static attribute will contribute to the JIT cache key, so with this strategy, if the floating point values change from one call to the next it will trigger re-compilation.

issue_title: Transposed preconditioned GMRES

conversation.text_input:
Description
I'm using jax.scipy.sparse.linalg.gmres with a preconditioner to solve some linear systems, and was trying to figure out why the forward solve would converge just fine but the gradient would not.
Looking through the code it looks like _solve closes over the preconditioner, so that the same preconditioner is used for the forward and backward pass:

  
    
      jax/jax/_src/scipy/sparse/linalg.py
    
    
        Lines 698 to 700
      in
      e04cc28
    
  
  
    

        
          
           def _solve(A, b): 
        

        
          
             return _gmres_solve(A, b, x0, atol, ptol, restart, maxiter, M, gmres_func) 
        

        
          
           x = lax.custom_linear_solve(A, b, solve=_solve, transpose_solve=_solve) 
        
    
  


Assuming the preconditioner satisfies $M A \sim I$, there's no reason that $M A^T \sim I$ unless $A$ is symmetric (which it usually isn't for GMRES).
I think the correct thing to do would be to define a separate _transpose_solve that uses the transpose of the preconditioner, since if $M A \sim I$ then $M^T A^T \sim I$ as well.
(also note that I think this is an issue for jax.scipy.sparse.linalg.bicgstab as well. cg is fine because $A$ is symmetric)

We might need a separate argument for passing a preconditioner to transposed solve.

conversation.output:
Wouldn't it be A T M T ∼ I ? So M T would be a right-side preconditioner instead of a left-sdie preconditioner. Not sure exactly how that changes the numerics, but it may not be a drop in replacement.

Strictly speaking this would be correct, but in practice I don't think you need to swap the side of the preconditioner. For cg the convergence behavior only depends on the eigenvalues, and $AB$ has the same spectrum as $BA$ so left and right preconditioning are the same. For gmres and bicgstab the convergence depends on both the eigenvalues and eigenvectors, so it can be slightly different for left and right preconditioned systems, but in practice there's usually little difference so which side to precondition is more of an implementation detail rather than theoretical (see eg Saad, (2003). Iterative methods for sparse linear systems). Assuming it converges, the results should be the same for either left or right preconditioned systems. (and in the limit of the "ideal preconditioner" $M = A^{-1}$ then the side doesn't matter either since $A$ always commutes with it's inverse.
I'm familiar with lineax, this bug was found when I was doing some benchmarking between the two. They were previously dropping the preconditoner entirely for the transposed solve which caused other issues, but it's recently been updated to use the transpose of the preconditioner, without swapping sides: patrick-kidger/lineax#162

issue_title: Reverse mode through JVP of vmapped function returns "TypeError: [...] <class 'jax._src.ad_util.Zero'> is not a valid JAX type"

conversation.text_input:
Description
When I run the following code I get the error:  TypeError: Value Zero(ShapedArray(float32[1,3])) with type <class 'jax._src.ad_util.Zero'> is not a valid JAX type on the grad_f_x = jax.jacrev(f)(x) line.
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp


def g(x):
    def p(z):
        return jnp.linalg.solve(z.sum()*jnp.eye(3), jnp.array([1., 0., 0.]))[0]

    h = lambda y: jax.jvp(jax.vmap(p), (x,), (y,))[1]

    return h

def f(x):
    return jax.vjp(g(x), jnp.ones_like(x))[1](x)[0]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    x = jnp.array([200.0])
    f_x = f(x)
    print(f"f({x}) = {f_x}")

    grad_f_x = jax.jacrev(f)(x)
    print(f"grad_f({x}) = {grad_f_x}")

I believe the issue is to do with the A in jnp.linalg.solve depending on z. If I move this to the b argument (or remove it), remove the vmap in h or replace h with h = lambda y: jax.vmap(p)(x*y) then the issue disappears. So it has to do with a combination of these elements.
I can also replace p with the following to remove the problem:
def p(z):
    return jax.lax.custom_linear_solve(
              lambda r: (z.sum()*jnp.eye(3)) @ r, 
              jnp.array([1., 0., 0.]),
              lambda mv_fn_, b_: jnp.linalg.solve(mv_fn_(jnp.eye(3)), b_),
              symmetric=True 
          )[0]

import functools
from typing import Callable

import chex
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from optax._src import base
import optax.tree


class Gumbel:
  """Gumbel distribution."""

  def sample(
      self,
      key: jax.typing.ArrayLike,
      sample_shape: base.Shape,
      dtype: jax.typing.DTypeLike = float,
  ) -> jax.Array:
    return jax.random.gumbel(key, sample_shape, dtype)

  def log_prob(self, inputs: jax.Array) -> jax.Array:
    return -inputs - jnp.exp(-inputs)


def make_perturbed_fun(
    fun: Callable[[chex.ArrayTree], chex.ArrayTree],
    num_samples: int = 1000,
    sigma: float = 0.1,
    noise=Gumbel(),
) -> Callable[[chex.ArrayTree, chex.PRNGKey], chex.ArrayTree]:
  def _compute_residuals(
      primal_in: chex.ArrayTree, rng: chex.PRNGKey
  ) -> tuple[chex.ArrayTree, chex.ArrayTree]:
    # random noise Zs to be added to inputs
    samples = optax.tree.random_like(rng,
        optax.tree.batch_shape(primal_in, (num_samples,)), sampler=noise.sample)

    # creates [inputs + Z_1, ..., inputs + Z_num_samples]
    primal_in_samples = jax.vmap(lambda z: optax.tree.add_scale(primal_in, sigma, z))(samples)

    # applies fun: [fun(inputs + Z_1), ..., fun(inputs + Z_num_samples)]
    primal_out_samples = jax.vmap(fun)(primal_in_samples)
    return primal_out_samples, samples

  @functools.partial(jax.custom_jvp,nondiff_argnums=(1,))
  def fun_perturb(primal_in: chex.ArrayTree, rng: chex.PRNGKey) -> chex.ArrayTree:
    primal_out_samples, _ = _compute_residuals(primal_in, rng)
    # average the perturbed outputs
    return jax.tree.map(lambda x: jnp.mean(x, axis=0), primal_out_samples)

  @fun_perturb.defjvp
  def fun_perturb_jvp(
          rng: chex.PRNGKey, primal_in: chex.ArrayTree, tangent_in: chex.ArrayTree
  ) -> chex.ArrayTree:
    assert len(primal_in) == 1 and len(tangent_in) == 1
    primal_in = primal_in[0]
    tangent_in = tangent_in[0]

    outputs_pert, samples = _compute_residuals(primal_in, rng)
    primal_out = jax.tree.map(lambda x: jnp.mean(x, axis=0), outputs_pert)

    tree_log_prob_func = lambda sample: optax.tree.sum(jax.tree.map(noise.log_prob, sample))
    @functools.partial(jax.vmap,in_axes=(0,0))
    def sample_tangent_out(output_pert, sample):
      _, grad_inner_prod = jax.jvp(tree_log_prob_func, (sample,), (tangent_in,))
      return jax.tree.map(lambda x: x * grad_inner_prod, output_pert)

    tangent_out_samples = sample_tangent_out(outputs_pert, samples)
    tangent_out = jax.tree.map(lambda x: -1/sigma * jnp.mean(x, axis=0), tangent_out_samples)

    return primal_out, tangent_out

  return fun_perturb

if __name__ == "__main__":
  def one_hot_argmax(inputs: jnp.ndarray) -> jnp.ndarray:
    """An argmax one-hot function for arbitrary shapes."""
    inputs_flat = jnp.reshape(inputs, (-1))
    flat_one_hot = jax.nn.one_hot(jnp.argmax(inputs_flat), inputs_flat.shape[0])
    return jnp.reshape(flat_one_hot, inputs.shape)

  def argmax_tree(x):
    return jax.tree.map(one_hot_argmax, x)

  sigma, num_samples = 2.0, 10_000
  key = jax.random.key(0)
  key, key1 = jax.random.split(key)
  x = jax.random.normal(key1, (20,))

  # pert_argmax_fun and its jacobian should be an unbiased estimator of
  # softmax_fun and its jacobian
  pert_argmax_fun = jax.jit(make_perturbed_fun(
      argmax_tree, num_samples, sigma))
  softmax_fun = lambda x: jax.tree.map(lambda z: jax.nn.softmax(z / sigma), x)

  expected = softmax_fun(x)
  got = pert_argmax_fun(x, key)
  chex.assert_trees_all_equal_shapes(got, expected)
  chex.assert_trees_all_close(got, expected, atol=1e-1)

  expected = jax.jacobian(softmax_fun)(x)
  got = jax.jacobian(pert_argmax_fun, argnums=0)(x, key)

        optax.tree.batch_shape(primal_in, (num_samples,)), sampler=noise.sample)

    # creates [inputs + Z_1, ..., inputs + Z_num_samples]
    primal_in_samples = jax.vmap(lambda z: optax.tree.add_scale(primal_in, sigma, z))(samples)

    # applies fun: [fun(inputs + Z_1), ..., fun(inputs + Z_num_samples)]
    primal_out_samples = jax.vmap(fun)(primal_in_samples)
    return primal_out_samples, samples

  @functools.partial(jax.custom_jvp,nondiff_argnums=(1,))
  def fun_perturb(primal_in: chex.ArrayTree, rng: chex.PRNGKey) -> chex.ArrayTree:
    primal_out_samples, _ = _compute_residuals(primal_in, rng)
    # average the perturbed outputs
    return jax.tree.map(lambda x: jnp.mean(x, axis=0), primal_out_samples)

  @fun_perturb.defjvp
  def fun_perturb_jvp(
          rng: chex.PRNGKey, primal_in: chex.ArrayTree, tangent_in: chex.ArrayTree
  ) -> chex.ArrayTree:
    assert len(primal_in) == 1 and len(tangent_in) == 1
    primal_in = primal_in[0]
    tangent_in = tangent_in[0]

    outputs_pert, samples = _compute_residuals(primal_in, rng)
    primal_out = jax.tree.map(lambda x: jnp.mean(x, axis=0), outputs_pert)

    tree_log_prob_func = lambda sample: optax.tree.sum(jax.tree.map(noise.log_prob, sample))
    @functools.partial(jax.vmap,in_axes=(0,0))
    def sample_tangent_out(output_pert, sample):
      _, grad_inner_prod = jax.jvp(tree_log_prob_func, (sample,), (tangent_in,))
      return jax.tree.map(lambda x: x * grad_inner_prod, output_pert)

    tangent_out_samples = sample_tangent_out(outputs_pert, samples)
    tangent_out = jax.tree.map(lambda x: -1/sigma * jnp.mean(x, axis=0), tangent_out_samples)

    return primal_out, tangent_out

  return fun_perturb

if __name__ == "__main__":
  def one_hot_argmax(inputs: jnp.ndarray) -> jnp.ndarray:
    """An argmax one-hot function for arbitrary shapes."""
    inputs_flat = jnp.reshape(inputs, (-1))
    flat_one_hot = jax.nn.one_hot(jnp.argmax(inputs_flat), inputs_flat.shape[0])
    return jnp.reshape(flat_one_hot, inputs.shape)

  def argmax_tree(x):
    return jax.tree.map(one_hot_argmax, x)

  sigma, num_samples = 2.0, 10_000
  key = jax.random.key(0)
  key, key1 = jax.random.split(key)
  x = jax.random.normal(key1, (20,))

  # pert_argmax_fun and its jacobian should be an unbiased estimator of
  # softmax_fun and its jacobian
  pert_argmax_fun = jax.jit(make_perturbed_fun(
      argmax_tree, num_samples, sigma))
  softmax_fun = lambda x: jax.tree.map(lambda z: jax.nn.softmax(z / sigma), x)

  expected = softmax_fun(x)
  got = pert_argmax_fun(x, key)
  chex.assert_trees_all_equal_shapes(got, expected)
  chex.assert_trees_all_close(got, expected, atol=1e-1)

  expected = jax.jacobian(softmax_fun)(x)
  got = jax.jacobian(pert_argmax_fun, argnums=0)(x, key)

conversation.output:
I dug a bit into this, and I have a workaround (#29362), but I am not sure it is the best way to deal with this. I have a somewhat smaller repro:
    def outer_fn(x):
      def inner_fn(x):
        return jax.jit(
            lambda x: lax.platform_dependent(x,
                                             default=jnp.sin,
                                             other=jnp.cos))(x)

      _, lin_fn = jax.linearize(inner_fn, x)

      def with_transpose(x):
        grad = jax.linear_transpose(lin_fn, x)(x)
        del grad
        return x

      return jax.lax.cond(x[0][0] > 0., with_transpose, lambda x: x, x)

    jax.vmap(outer_fn)(jnp.ones((5, 10, 10)))

the error is AssertionError: The index of a cond with branches_platforms should be a platform_index and should never be mapped and it arises because batching is not implemented for a cond where there is a branches_platforms param and the cond index is batched (see here).
These cond were introduced in #28607 to represent lax.platform_dependent, and they are used as follows:
  idx = platform_index[platforms=PPP]
  res = cond {branches = ..., branches_platforms=PPP} idx ...

When applying batching to a Jaxpr like the above the output of platform_index will be considered unbatched, because it does not have any inputs. This works!
But when we apply linearize we are doing partial_eval of a Jaxpr like the above, and the output of platform_index is considered known (since it has no inputs, hence all inputs are known), and is considered a residual. The whole unknown Jaxpr then takes the idx as an input, and when applying batching it will be batched. This results in failure in the cond batching rule.
I have attempted to change how partial eval works for platform_index, to mark its output as unknown, so that it is recomputed, thus ensuring that the subsequent cond is always accompanied by platform_index. This resulted in a bunch of invariants  of partial eval being broken.
My best attempt at the moment is #29362, where upon encountering a cond with batched index and with branches_platforms, I replace the index with a fresh call to platform_index_p. This is possible because the branches_platforms param of the cond is all we need to recompute the platform index.

conversation.output:
This is behaving as expected: bfloat16 is a very low-precision data type: it only has seven bits of mantissa, meaning that it can distinguish values to about 1 part in 128 on average. The spacing between representable values in the region you're asking about can be seen with the jnp.spacing function:
>>> import jax.numpy as jnp
>>> jnp.spacing(jnp.bfloat16(1.04858e+06))
Array(8192, dtype=bfloat16)
This tells you that the next representable value differs by 8192, so when you add 2032 you're well within the range that rounds down to the original value.
If you're hoping for more precise computations in this region, you'll have to use a higher-precision data type, such as float32.

issue_title: `scipy.cluster.hierarchy.linkage`: slowness when chaining `jax.pure_callback`

conversation.text_input:
Description
scipy.cluster.hierarchy.linkage is very slow on JAX CPU compared to NumPy, exhibiting big-O performance that is ~52% the speed of NumPy: scipy/scipy#22246 (comment)
The function is implemented in Cython; internally it chains two calls to jax.pure_callback. The first call returns an array of size ~n^2, which is consumed by the second call.
Here's a minimal reproducer that simulates calling linkage(y, method='simple') on an input of shape (6162, 2), on NumPy and on JAX.
The POC demonstrates three unjustified elements of slowness in JAX:

187ms delay between the end of the first callback and the start of the second one;
74ms to call jax.Array.__array__(copy=False) on a 144 MiB array, which should be a view;
24ms between the exit of the second callback and when .block_until_ready returns.

import time

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)
jax.config.update("jax_default_device", jax.devices("cpu")[0])

y = np.random.random((6162, 2))
jy = jnp.asarray(y).block_until_ready()

def _np_pdist(y):
    print(f"{time.time():.3f} enter _np_pdist")
    d = np.random.random((18982041, ))
    print(f"{time.time():.3f} exit _np_pdist")
    return d

def _jnp_pdist(y):
    print(f"{time.time():.3f} enter _jnp_pdist")
    y = np.asarray(y, copy=False)
    d = _np_pdist(y)
    d = jnp.asarray(d)
    print(f"{time.time():.3f} exit _jnp_pdist")
    return d

def cy_linkage(d):
    print(f"{time.time():.3f} enter cy_linkage")
    l = np.random.random((6161, 4))
    print(f"{time.time():.3f} exit cy_linkage")
    return l

def jnp_linkage(d):
    print(f"{time.time():.3f} enter jnp_linkage")
    d = np.asarray(d, copy=False)
    l = cy_linkage(d)
    l = jnp.asarray(l)
    print(f"{time.time():.3f} exit jnp_linkage")
    return l

def linkage(y):
    d = _np_pdist(y)
    l = cy_linkage(d)
    return l

@jax.jit
def jax_linkage(y):
    d = jax.pure_callback(
        _jnp_pdist,
        jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((18982041, ), jnp.float64),
        y,
    )
    l = jax.pure_callback(
        jnp_linkage,
        jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((6161, 4), jnp.float64),
        d,
    )
    return l

_ = jax_linkage(jy).block_until_ready()  # warm up JIT


print(f"{time.time():.3f} start NumPy benchmark")
linkage(y)
print(f"{time.time():.3f} end NumPy benchmark")

print(f"{time.time():.3f} start JAX benchmark")

issue_title: custom_partitioning compatibility with lax.composite

conversation.text_input:
We’ve encountered a compatibility issue between lax.composite and jax.experimental.custom_partitioning. Currently, scaled_matmul (see source) is implemented using a primitive with custom_partitioning. We are now migrating this to use lax.composite (see PR).
The issue arises because XLA expects the input to be annotated as a composite. However, once wrapped with custom_partitioning, the op becomes a stablehlo.custom_call @CustomSPMDPartitioning, and the composite annotation is lost. This breaks downstream transformations that rely on composite structure.
Since scaled_matmul has many sharding scenarios, lax.composite offers substantial benefits in terms of pattern matching and rewrite flexibility within XLA.
Is there a recommended way to define custom partitioning rules for a composite while preserving its annotation through to XLA? @kaixih @sergachev @nouiz @hawkinsp
A mini-reproducer can be found:
from jax import lax
from jax._src.custom_partitioning import custom_partitioning
from functools import partial
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from jax.sharding import NamedSharding, PartitionSpec
from jax.experimental import mesh_utils

devices = mesh_utils.create_device_mesh((4,))
mesh = jax.sharding.Mesh(devices, axis_names=('x',))
sharding = NamedSharding(mesh, PartitionSpec('x'))

x = jnp.arange(80, dtype=jnp.float32)
y = jnp.arange(80, dtype=jnp.float32)

x_sharded = jax.device_put(x, sharding)
y_sharded = jax.device_put(y, sharding)

@partial(lax.composite,name="ns.my_composite")
def custom_composite(x, y, /, *, axis=0):  # Note: positional-only and keyword-only args
    """Example composite operation combining multiple lax operations."""
    z = x * y 
    w = z + x

issue_title: Incorrect Differentiation of sign(x)*log(abs(x) + 1)

conversation.text_input:
The function sign(x)*log(abs(x) + 1) is composed of non-differentiable functions, but in fact it is differentiable everywhere.
The derivative wrt x is 0*log(abs(x) + 1) + sign(x)^2 / (abs(x) + 1) = 1 / (abs(x) + 1)
In JAX, it appears that it cannot correctly identify the fact that sign(x)^2  = 1 and instead computes sign(x) twice and multiplies the result. When x = 0, this is wrong. I have attached a minimal example of what I'm talking about. The printed output should be 1, but instead the function returns zero.
import jax

def f(x):
    return jax.numpy.sign(x)*jax.numpy.log(jax.numpy.abs(x) + 1)
        
print(jax.jacfwd(f)(0.0))

Of course, this issue can be solved by defining a custom jvp, but that seems wrong since the root cause is an incorrect calculation.
Perhaps the best way is to do a custom jvp, but I thought I should post here in case there is an easy patch.
conversation.output:

In JAX, it appears that it cannot correctly identify the fact that sign(x)^2 = 1

I think this statement is incorrect. When x = 0, then jnp.sign(x) = 0 and jnp.sign(x) ** 2 = 0, not 1. Could that be the source of the discrepancy you're seeing?

issue_title: jax.numpy.logaddexp2 yields large errors with bfloat16/float16 inputs

conversation.text_input:
Description
The current implementation of jax.numpy.logaddexp2 appears to produce significant numerical errors when using bfloat16/float16 inputs. This seems to stem from how the function is implemented:
@binary_ufunc(identity=-np.inf, reduce=reductions._logsumexp2)
def logaddexp2(x1: ArrayLike, x2: ArrayLike, /) -> Array:
  x1, x2 = promote_args_inexact("logaddexp2", x1, x2)
  ln2 = float(np.log(2))
  return logaddexp(x1 * ln2, x2 * ln2) / ln2

Since bfloat16/float16 has very limited precision, the intermediate scaling with log(2) and division may introduce noticeable numerical error.
Here is a minimal reproducible example that demonstrates the problem:
import numpy as np
import jax.numpy as jnp


def test(dtype):
    x = [-1.40625, -2.32812, -0.769531, -0.71875, -0.851562, -0.878906, -0.417969, -0.527344, 0.921875]
    y = [0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 3, 0, 2, 4]


    x_np = np.array(x, dtype)
    y_np = np.array(y, dtype)

    x_jnp = jnp.array(x, dtype)
    y_jnp = jnp.array(y, dtype)

    x_jnp_float32 = jnp.array(x, 'float32')
    y_jnp_float32 = jnp.array(y, 'float32')

    np_res = np.logaddexp2(x_np, y_np)
    jnp_res = jnp.logaddexp2(x_jnp, y_jnp)
    jnp_res_float32 = jnp.logaddexp2(x_jnp_float32, y_jnp_float32)


    jnp_error = jnp.linalg.norm(jnp_res - jnp_res_float32)
    np_error = jnp.linalg.norm(np_res - jnp_res_float32)
    
    print(f'{dtype}, jnp error: {jnp_error}')
    print(f'{dtype},  np error: {np_error}')
    print(f'{dtype}, jnp/np error ratio: {jnp_error / np_error}')


test('float16')
test('bfloat16')

def logaddexp2(x1, x2):

A quick comment on this: NumPy does not have any native float16/bfloat16 execution paths; rather it performs the computation in float64 (I believe) and then casts the result to float16/bfloat16. So comparison between JAX and NumPy is somewhat unfair: NumPy is accumulating errors at 64-bit precision, while JAX is accumulating float errors at 16-bit precision. With that in mind, the current behavior of JAX is about what you'd expect, given that bfloat16 only has 7 mantissa bits.
All that to say, I'm happy to do the work to marginally improve the logaddexp2 implementation in extreme cases, but none of the results above strike me as particularly problematic: in general when you work with bfloat16 you should expect loss of precision at this level.

import jax
from jax.experimental import pallas as pl
from jax.experimental.pallas import tpu as pltpu
import jax.numpy as jnp


def bcast_matvec(a, b):
    # a is [batch_bcast..., contract]
    # b is [batch_bcast..., contract, out]
    # returns [batch_bcast..., out]
    assert a.ndim == b.ndim - 1
    pet = dict(preferred_element_type="float32")
    if b.shape[-3] == 1:
        # this means we're bcasting the last dim of a, so we can use
        # it in matmul dims.
        return jnp.matmul(a, jnp.squeeze(b, -3), **pet)
    return jnp.squeeze(
        jnp.matmul(jnp.expand_dims(a, -2), b, **pet),
        -2,
    )


def kernel(a, b, c, out):
    p1 = bcast_matvec(a[...], b[...])
    p2 = bcast_matvec(p1.astype(a.dtype), c[...])
    out[...] = p2.astype(a.dtype)


def linear_block(_shape) -> pl.BlockSpec:
    shape = list(_shape)
    assert len(shape) >= 3
    shape[0] = None  # pl.Squeezed()
    # index_map turns grid index into block index
    index_map = lambda j: tuple([j] + ([0] * (len(shape) - 1)))
    return pl.BlockSpec(tuple(shape), index_map)


def random_array(shape, dtype, key=2025):
    return jax.random.normal(jax.random.PRNGKey(key), shape, dtype=dtype)


def run(dtype):

    s = 2
    t = 2
    u = 4
    d = 8

    b_shape = (r, t, 1, d, s)
    c_shape = (r, t, 1, s, d)
    out_shape = (t, u, d)

    func = pl.pallas_call(
        kernel,
        grid=(r,),
        in_specs=[
            pl.BlockSpec(a_shape, None),
            linear_block(b_shape),
            linear_block(c_shape),
        ],
        out_shape=jax.ShapeDtypeStruct(out_shape, dtype=dtype),
    )

    out = func(
        random_array(a_shape, dtype),
        random_array(b_shape, dtype),
        random_array(c_shape, dtype),
    )

def main():

issue_title: JAX/FALX.NNX: TypeError - JVPTracer for scalar nnx.Param incorrectly treated as compile-time constant in nested transformations (jit + value_and_grad)

conversation.text_input:
Description
When using flax.nnx with nested JAX transformations (specifically nnx.jit applied to a function that internally calls nnx.value_and_grad), a scalar nnx.Param (or a nnx.Param with shape (1,)) can cause a TypeError. The error indicates that a JVPTracer associated with this parameter is being incorrectly treated as a compile-time constant by JAX's JIT machinery.
This issue was identified when a JVPTracer for a scalar float32 parameter (e.g., Traced<ShapedArray(float32[])> or Traced<ShapedArray(float32)>) appeared in jaxpr.consts during the lowering to MLIR phase, leading to an InvalidInputException and subsequently a TypeError. The problem is reproducible with the minimal example below.
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import flax.nnx as nnx

class InnerModule(nnx.Module):
  def __init__(self, *, rngs: nnx.Rngs):
    # The error occurs with a scalar nnx.Param
    self.alpha = nnx.Param(jnp.array(0.0, dtype=jnp.float32)) # Scalar

I think there is incompatibility between libcusparse version required by jax wheels and libnvjitlink version available in your system.
The ELF files in jax wheels have the RPATH tag set in NEEDED section (you can check it via readelf --dynamic <path to ELF file>). dlopen() searches RPATH first (if set), then LD_LIBRARY_PATH, then RUNPATH (see https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/dlopen.3.html)
What happened here is that the libraries required by jax wheels were found in correct location (via RPATH pointing to NVIDIA pypi wheels installation). However, libcusparse.so.12 (which is not controlled by JAX) uses RUNPATH, and when dlopen() was searching for libnvJitLink.so.12 location, RUNPATH value got overriden by LD_LIBRARY_PATH on your system.
So the libcusparse version was correct, and libnvjitlink version was old and incompatible with libcusparse.
So yes, I suggest not using LD_LIBRARY_PATH if you use JAX.

issue_title: Mutiplicative rules for hessian fail for user defined jvps.

conversation.text_input:
Description
The following is a simple example: with custom jvp rules that doesn't match with the deduced ones, higher order automatic differential rules are generated from the custom jvp procedure. However, the multiplicative rules (including pows) fail to deduce the correct result.
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
@jax.custom_jvp
def foo(x: jax.Array):
    return jnp.ones_like(x)

@foo.defjvp
def foo_jvp(primals: jax.Array, tangents: jax.Array):
    x, = primals
    x_dot, = tangents
    return jnp.ones_like(x), x * x_dot

def fun(x):
    return foo(x) ** 2

x = jnp.array(0.5)
print(x)
print(jax.jacfwd(fun)(x))
print(jax.hessian(fun)(x))
Result: 0.5 1.0 2.0
Expected: 0.5 1.0 2.5
For those unfamiliar with higher-order AD:
Using generalized dual number algebra, namely $R[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^n)$, up to $n-1$ th differential rules (or jets) can be defined. A simple example is where $n=3$, then the algebra can be expressed as the algebra on $x+v\epsilon+\frac{u}{2}\epsilon^2$ with $\epsilon^3=0$. Then taylor-mode AD tells us that $f(x+v\epsilon+\frac{u}{2}\epsilon^2)=f(x)+\partial f(x)[v]\epsilon+\frac{1}{2}(\partial f(x)[u] + \partial^2 f(x)[v,v])\epsilon^2$
With that notation, $foo(x+\epsilon)=1+x\epsilon+\frac{1}{2}\epsilon^2$, so $fun(x+\epsilon)$ should be $1+2x\epsilon+\frac{1}{2}(2x^2+2)\epsilon^2$. But jax-deduced result only captures the $2$ part in hessian. Fun fact is that torch-deduced ones (with torch.func) only captures the $2x^2$ part. Thought this might be a general problem so posted here.

jaxlib: 0.5.3

If you want foo and its custom derivative rule around for the second AD pass, you need to have it present in output of the first pass, i.e. to compute the primal outputs in its own JVP rule. It's discussed in the tutorial:

NotImplementedError: sparse rule for reduce_max is not implemented.
Minimal Reproducible Example
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from jax.experimental import sparse

@jax.experimental.sparse.sparsify
def test(matrix):
    return jnp.max(jnp.abs(matrix))

M = sparse.BCOO.fromdense(-jnp.arange(12).reshape(3, 4))

# Works fine with dense input
M_dense = -jnp.arange(12).reshape(3, 4)
print(test(M_dense))
conversation.output: Thanks for the report! in general reduce_max over a sparse structure is essentially equivalent to a group-by reduction over the data buffer with respect to the index buffer, and there's not really any efficient code path for such an operation in XLA: I think this is the main reason this operation hasn't been implemented yet.

issue_title: pytest: use importlib mode

conversation.text_input:
Description
#28650 attempted to do this, but it was rolled back in #28690 due to #28671.
Motivation for the change:

Otherwise the default (prepend) mode will add <jax_src_dir>/tests and <jax_src_dir> to the start of sys.path.
This is (has always been) fragile, because <jax_src_dir> has jax/ and jaxlib/ subdirectories, but it recently broke as setuptools 80 has a change in behaviour for editable installations, with the result that if jaxlib is installed editable then import jaxlib with <jax_src_dir> in sys.path will try to import from <jax_src_dir>/jaxlib instead of the editable install location, and fail.
See also:

https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/explanation/pythonpath.html#import-modes
https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/explanation/goodpractices.html#tests-outside-application-code (JAX does not follow the advice here, as there is not a src/ directory alongside tests/ at the top level)

issue_title: Provide wheel for Windows ARM64

conversation.text_input:
What is the current behavior?
Unable to install the package from pip.
What is the desired behavior?
To have native wheel for WoA. GitHub Actions now supports win-arm64 for free.
How would this improve jax and jaxlib?
Due to the library's popularity, a native version for the growing number of Windows on ARM (WoA) devices offers a better user experience.
conversation.output:
Thanks for the request! We don't currently have the infrastructure in place to test or build ARM wheels for Windows, but we're always happy to help if folks run into issues building from source (it's possible that that already works!), or if there is community interest in supporting such wheels.
Let's keep this feature request open, and we can track the community's interest in/need for wheels for Windows ARM.

issue_title: Allow for passing slices of indices to `*_argnum` style arguments

conversation.text_input:
Sometimes, when defining functions with many arguments, we need to specify something like nondiff_argnums or static_argnums for many of its arguments. This leads to quite long lists of indices to specify them all. I guess this is required in the backend to have a concrete array of values, but I feel there is nothing stopping us adding a thin wrapper to convert a more ergnomic format into the concrete array of values.
Concrete example:
fn: callable = ... # a function with many arguments
jit_fn = jax.jit(fn, static_argnums=(1,2,3,4,5,6,7))
What if we instead could support a slice object?
fn: callable = ... # a function with many arguments
jit_fn = jax.jit(fn, static_argnums=slice(1, 7))
or a custom tuple format, say:
fn: callable = ... # a function with many arguments
jit_fn = jax.jit(fn, static_argnums=(1, ..., 7))
or something of a similar vein. Ideally we could have something like 1:7 but I don't think the python interpreter allows this!
This is mostly for ergonomics, and also to avoid bugs where we add an additional argument, but forget to update the static argnum. We can instead leave an open range in the slice to include all additional arguments:
fn: callable = ... # a function with many arguments
jit_fn = jax.jit(fn, static_argnums=slice(1, None))

# or

jit_fn = jax.jit(fn, static_argnums=(1, ...))
In the library itself, these can be trivially converted to a concrete list of the actual argnums.
What do you think?

I am aware of the existence of *_argname variants to some functions. But these don't cover all cases nor does it exist on all functions (such as custom_vjp)
conversation.output: It's an interesting idea – I lean toward not making this change, because the clarity of the explicit tuple is useful. I'll note that even in your motivating example, you had an off-by-one error: slice(1, 7) conventionally does not include the value 7.

 https://github.com/jax-ml/jax/blob/0e690c1a88049787f8371d462d674a94f9b85c73/jaxlib/pytree.h#L128-L130

 I have to admit that the inner workings of absl::Hash are somewhat opaque
 to me, but I know from experience that it doesn't always directly call
 __hash__ for the object that is passed to it.

 Equality checks are a bit more transparent I think, though it's not a
 matter of simply checking if a == b in Python. It's implemented in
 nanobind here:
 https://github.com/jax-ml/jax/blob/0e690c1a88049787f8371d462d674a94f9b85c73/jaxlib/pytree.cc#L271-L293
 We could probably add some logic here to change which error is raised when
 objects without valid equality semantics are marked as static parameters,
 but it wouldn't be much more than adding an addendum to the existing error
 that's something like "make sure the static parameters of your pytree have
 valid equality semantics".

issue_title: For implementation of QR decomposition, lower to `stablehlo.composite` vs. `stablehlo.custom_call` for custom backends

conversation.text_input:
Currently, JAX lowers jax.lax.linalg.qr into a composistion of more primitive lapack-like operations  geeqf and orgqr.
For backends other than CPU/GPU backends, these kernels are emitted as stablehlo.custom_call @Qr and stablehlo.custom_call @ProductOfElementaryHouseholderReflectors.
In XLA, the QR Expander Pass allows XLA to insert explicit computation for qeqrf (stablehlo.custom_call @Qr) and the ProductOfElementaryHouseholderReflectors.
If instead JAX emitted stablehlo.composite, then the expansions for the kernels could also be emitted, preserving the ability to offload to a library call while also providing the backup implementation.

Hi @dfm, thanks for the response.
My perspective is from implementing a PJRT plugin. Currently, when we receive StableHLO for a JAX program through PJRT, the jax.lax.inalg.qr is decomposed into more primitive operations, including the two custom calls to @Qr and @ProductOfElementaryHouseholderReflectors.
But there's nothing in the StableHLO specification about what these two custom calls @Qr and @ProductOfElementaryHouseholderReflectors are supposed to mean. Instead, PJRT plugin authors need to look into JAX or XLA code to figure it out.
Since XLA provides default a default decomposition for both of these operations in its QrExpander pass, and this pass is used in both CPU, GPU, and interpreter pipelines, I thought it might be reasonable to suggest that the same logic could instead be moved to the JAX side (in Python) to provide a side definition for @Qr and @ProductOfElementaryHouseholderReflectors while still preserving them as separate functions. In this manner, backends can use the "default" (but possibly poorly performing implementation) or they can easily match and replace the symbols with their own implementation. Based on my understanding, this is what stablehlo.composite is supposed to enable.

could you write a backend-specific lowering rule

I actually didn't know that this was possible. If my PJRT plugin can register custom lowerings for jax.linalg.qr  such that those lowerings are automatically registered via the plugin's Python initialization code, then that would probably work.

As far as I understand, the @Qr and @ProductOfElementaryHouseholderReflectors custom calls are really only meant as part of the TPU plugin contract, and on CPU and GPU the QrExpander pass must be a no-op! I expect that the reason why you see these custom calls for your custom backend (instead of an error) is because the TPU lowering rule is registered as the default fallback rule, e.g.:

  
    
      jax/jax/_src/lax/linalg.py
    
    
         Line 1757
      in
      f73726e
    
  
  
    

        
          
           mlir.register_lowering(geqrf_p, _geqrf_lowering_rule) 
        
    
  


Which doesn't seem like great behavior to me, for all the reasons that you've already laid out. I think this should probably just error loudly, rather than generating poorly defined custom calls for arbitrary backends!
So concretely, I think that the best short term approach would probably be to register a platform-specific lowering (e.g. mlir.register_lowering(lax.linalg.geqrf_p, custom_lowering, platform="my_backend")) that emits the HLO that you need for your use case. You could even register a custom lowering for qr_p directly, which currently unconditionally lowers to the two other primitives here. If you want to try this, I'm very happy to help iron out any issues you hit along the way!
That being said, there are some possible longer term approaches that could be feasible, but I'm not sure that they are necessarily good ideas:


There is an argument to be made that StableHLO could include more linear algebra operations in the spec, since it already includes Cholesky decomposition, and triangular solves. This is something that @hawkinsp has thought about, but I think the general feeling is that it's not really worth the maintenance burden for backend developers. (It's also often useful for us as JAX developers to use custom calls for things like this since we explicitly own the kernels.)


Another option (as you have suggested) might be to lower our linear algebra operations to composite ops, with explicit expanded default implementations. As you've already pointed out, it might be feasible to do this for QR already (I've heard that @hawkinsp actually originally wrote the QrExpander pass in Python anyways!). I'm not convinced that this is a good idea, because the default implementation wasn't actually ever meant to be used, so I think it might be misleading to include it as the "decomposition" of such a composite op. That being said, if it would significantly helps plugin developers like yourself, I'm happy to continue chatting about ideas like this!

@justinjfu and I partially debugged this...
The pallas_call lowering errs with the message about interpret mode whenever we lower a pallas_call on CPU without interpret mode.
In some contexts, we lower every one of the per-platform rules handed to lax.platform_dependent. Specifically, we emit an XLA switch and leave the right platform rule to be "selected as runtime" (more below).
We can illustrate this without lax.platform_dependent too, just a lax.cond:
from functools import partial
import jax, jax.numpy as jnp
from jax.experimental import pallas as pl

branch = partial(pl.pallas_call,
                 lambda _: None,
                 out_shape=jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((), jnp.int32))

def f(x):
  return x + jax.lax.cond(False,
                          lambda: branch(interpret=False)(),
                          lambda: branch(interpret=True)())

jax.jit(f)(1.)
We wrote "selected at runtime" in quotes above because, at some level, we actually know in principle what platform we're lowering for here. (That's because we're not only compiling for CPU, but also running on CPU, since we're using jax.jit, not an AOT or export path). Like the toy cond example above, you could say this is an issue where lowering (and the error-checking done in pallas_call lowering specifically) is too conservative or early.

conversation.output:
I think this is a problem with how platform_dependent is implemented. It relies on the fact that all branches can actually be lowered on all platforms. Once there is a lowering, it relies on constant and conditional folding that happens early in compilation to keep only the branch we need (compilation is always for a single platform, while tracing and lowering can defer the choice of the platform).
In JAX we do have primitives that can only be lowered for some platforms, so platform_dependent should have a way to deal with such primitives.
I need to think some more about a good solution. I have tried a while ago to make platform_dependent a primitive, which means that it has its own lowering rules, and can be smart about only lowering the branches that it needs. But this is quite complicated because it will need to handle all the things that conditional primitives in JAX handle. Turning it into a switch seemed to be able to leverage all the features of switch. Except that now switch reasonably expects all branches to be lowerable.

conversation.output:
I have started to look into this and I created #28607 so far containing a reproducing test. As the test shows, lax.platform_dependent operates in a confusing way because it lowers all branches for the current lowering platform. This is all fine if branches are lowerable for all platforms, but I think that is too strong of a requirement. (I am surprised that we did not run into this before, but most JAX primitives are lowerable on all platforms, pallas_call and a few linalg primitives such as eig are rare exceptions.)
Solution A: The cleanest solution may be creating a conditional primitive for platform_dependent. Then its lowering rule can do the right thing and only lower the branches that are needed. But JAX conditional primitives are very complicated to implement. A variant of this solution is to add some bits from platform_dependent to cond_p, and then customize the lowering of cond_p for the case when it is a conditional on platform index. wdyt?
Solution B: We can try to resolve platform_index during tracing, so that we don't even introduce a conditional. This is what was attempted in 
  
    
      jax/jax/_src/lax/control_flow/conditionals.py
    
    
        Lines 1076 to 1084
      in
      8137c37
    
  
  
    

        
          
           try: 
        

        
          
             # Note/TODO(mvoz): This actually rarely seems to concretize - we could look into 
        

        
          
             # core.ensure_compile_time_eval to get better single-branch selection. 
        

        
          
             platform_index_concrete = core.concrete_or_error(operator.index, platform_index) 
        

        
          
           except core.ConcretizationTypeError: 
        

        
          
             return switch(platform_index, branches, *args) 
        

        
          
           else: 
        

        
          
             assert 0 <= platform_index_concrete < len(branches) 
        

        
          
             return branches[platform_index_concrete](*args) 
        
    
  


but as we see this does not work in a staging context (jit, cond, scan, etc.). Furthermore, so far the tracing in JAX is platform independent and I think it is best to leave it like that.
Solution C: We could do some constant and conditional folding during or just before lowering, when we know the actual platforms we are lowering for. It turns out that the Jaxpr that platform_dependent generates is always of the following form:
   platform_idx = platform_index (platforms=...)
   clamped_platform_idx = clamp 0 platform_idx 1
   res = cond branches=(branch_0, branch_1) clamped_platform_idx

We could pattern-match on this and remove unnecessary branches. The implementation is not too bad, but it would cost another Jaxpr traveral. (To check if we already have such a pre-lowering traversal.) Note that we have to handle both
the single-platform lowering when platform_idx is resolved to a constant, but also the multi-platform lowering.
During single-platform lowering the platform_index will be resolved to a constant (either 0 or 1). We'd have to constant fold the clamp and then when we lower the cond we can special case it for when the index is a constant. E.g., we have a platform_dependent branch that can only be lowered for TPU, and we are in multi-platform lowering mode for CPU and CUDA. The constant-folding should remove all irrelevant branches.
This pattern matching could be brittle to changes in how we trace, but I think we can catch those in tests. Maybe, there could be other code transformations that could legitimately change the Jaxpr so that our constant folding is foiled. This would not be the case for batching and AD because platform_index has no dependencies and appears as a constant.

Simpler repro that does not involve JAX (except as a way to get MLIR):
from jax._src.lib.mlir import ir

import io
import concurrent.futures
import threading

num_workers = 40
num_runs = 20

barrier = threading.Barrier(num_workers)

aglobal = None

def module_to_bytecode(module: ir.Module) -> bytes:
  output = io.BytesIO()
  module.operation.write_bytecode(file=output)
  return output.getvalue()


def closure():
    global aglobal
    barrier.wait()

    for _ in range(num_runs):
        with ir.Context():
            loc = ir.Location.unknown()
            m = ir.Module.create(loc=loc)

        aglobal = m
        module_to_bytecode(aglobal)

with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=num_workers) as executor:
    for _ in range(100):
        futures = []
        for i in range(num_workers):
            futures.append(executor.submit(closure))
        assert len(list(f.result() for f in futures)) == num_workers

    t3 = %timeit -o -q -r 1 -n 1 betainc(a, b, jx_cpu).block_until_ready()  # warm JIT

issue_title: Use batched library routines when available.

conversation.text_input:
I recently performed some profiling comparing the tridiagonal solvers in jax (jax.lax.linalg.tridiagonal_solve) with  lineax. I observed that the jax call to the cusparse gtsv2 routine on GPU was much faster than the partially unrolled lineax implementation of the Thomas algorithm when unbatched or for small batch sizes. However, if I increase the batch size there is a crossover point at which lineax is faster because jax.lax.linalg scales ~linearly with batch-size and lineax scales sub-linearly/in constant time (and if I manually increase the unroll in lineax to fully unrolled then lineax is faster when any batch size).
I was looking at making a PR in lineax which used the best of both worlds, but then I started to wonder why the jax implementation did not scale as well. It turns out that the jax implementation does not use the cusparse batch implementations (i.e. cusparse<t>gtsv2StridedBatch() and cusparse<t>gtsvInterleavedBatch()). Instead it just performs a for loop over the batch dimensions.
My immediate objective is to get this addressed sooner rather than later to enable clean completion of my lineax PR that I don't need to change at a later date while improving or maintaining current performance. Note my current use case does not include batch solves (I am doing an implicit solve of the 1D heat equation). In the future I may perhaps want to use the batch solve for ADI, multi-group diffusion, or batched simulations.
I would be more than happy to help but I begin to lose track at the Python/C++ barrier when trawling through the source code.
I have worded the issue title in a very general way, if we just want it to refer to tridiagonal solves happy to rename.
